ety.text: PIE word *h₁néwn̥ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ Proto-Germanic *newunt Proto-Germanic *newun Proto-West Germanic *neun Proto-West Germanic *nigun Old English nigon Middle English nyn English nine From Middle English nyn, nyne, from Old English nigon (“nine”), from Proto-West Germanic *neun, from Proto-Germanic *newun (“nine”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ (“nine”).

senses.d: A numerical value equal to 9; the number following eight and preceding ten.
ex: Of course, for a number to have a biography, we need to assume that none of its digits are present more than nine times.

senses.d: Describing a group or set with nine elements.
ex: A cat has nine lives.

senses.d: The digit or figure 9.
A playing card with nine pips.
A nine-millimeter semi-automatic pistol.
A statistical unit of proportion (of reliability, purity, etc.), counting the number of digits nine in a percentage.
ex: They guaranteed that our Web site would have 99.99% uptime, or four nines.

senses.d: A baseball club, team, or lineup (composed of nine players).
ex: The St. Louis club is the only nine in the league which gives its patrons the right to see a full game or no pay.

grp.label: set or group with nine components

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French neuf, from Old French nuef, from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.
Inherited from Old Spanish nueve~nuef, from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἐννέα (ennéa), Portuguese nove, Old English nigon (English nine).
From Old Galician-Portuguese nove, from Latin novem (“nine”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Compare Spanish nueve.
Learned borrowing from Latin novēna. By surface analysis, nove (“nine”) + -ena.

phr: a stitch in time saves nine

ety.text: From Middle English nynthe, nynte, from Old English niġoþa, from Proto-Germanic *newundô; the -n- was reinserted by analogy with nine. Equivalent to nine + -th (ordinal suffix).

senses.d: The ordinal form of the number nine.
The person or thing in the ninth position.
One of nine equal parts of a whole.

The compound interval between any tone and the tone represented on the ninth degree of the staff above it, as between one of the scale and two of the octave above; the octave of the second, consisting of 13 or 14 semitones (called minor and major ninth).
To lose a ninth.
ex: A yearling "is ninthed" for Semele on Myconos (LSCG 96.23–24); the victim "is not ninthed" for Heracles Thasios

senses.d: To divide by nine.

grp.label: ordinal form of nine — see also 9th
one of nine equal parts of a whole

From Middle English nyntene, nynetene, from Old English niġontīene, niġontēne, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Cognate with Dutch negentien, Low German negenteihn, Hunsrik neinzen, German neunzehn, Danish nitten. Equivalent to nine + -teen

senses.d: The cardinal number occurring after eighteen and before twenty, represented in Roman numerals as XIX and in Arabic numerals as 19. It is the last/largest of the "teens".
ex: She says groovy like it's nineteen sixty-nine.

ety.text: Inherited from Latin decem ac novem (“ten and nine”). Compare Venetan disinove.
Inherited from Old Spanish dizenuef.
From Old Galician-Portuguese dez (“ten”) + e (“and”) + nove (“nine”).

From Middle English nynty, nynety, from Old English hundniġontiġ, from Proto-Germanic *newuntēhundą (“ninety”), equivalent to nine + -ty. Cognate with Scots nynty, nynety (“ninety”), Saterland Frisian njuugentich (“ninety”), West Frisian njoggentich (“ninety”), Dutch negentig (“ninety”), German Low German negentig (“ninety”), German neunzig (“ninety”), Swedish nittio (“ninety”), Norwegian Bokmål nitti (“ninety”), Norwegian Nynorsk nitti (“ninety”), Icelandic níutíu (“ninety”).

senses.d: The cardinal number occurring after eighty-nine and before ninety-one, represented in Roman numerals as XC and in Arabic numerals as 90.

Inherited from Old Spanish novaenta, from Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).

From décimo + noveno.

Borrowed from Japanese 忍者 (ninja), of uncertain derivation but with an underlying sense of secret or hidden person. Popularized in Japanese by manga after World War II and in English by the 1980 novel The Ninja by Eric Van Lustbader and the 1981 movie Enter the Ninja Noun sense 3.1 (“Mongolian miner”) arose from the supposed resemblance of the bowls used to wash ore with mercury to the shells of the main characters from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. The Juggalo slang sense arose via influence from AAVE nigga.

senses.d: One trained in ninjutsu, especially one used for espionage, assassination, and other tasks requiring stealth during Japan's shogunate period.
ex: He used to work in the Japanese agency as a ninja.
The men... are now learning to be ninja or ‘stealers-in’.

senses.d: One who very skillful, considered similar to the historical ninja, especially in covert or stealthy operation.
ex: Other bankers are dubbing themselves ninja, modern-day descendants of the superspies of 17th century samurai houses.
A JavaScript ninja should write lots of code and build things!

senses.d: A notional draconian arm of a corporation (originally Nintendo), tasked with dealing with individuals that infringe on its rights or do not comply with its regulations.
ex: I had TOTK running on my pc 2 weeks before it released on the switch and I'm still here. They can send the ninjas, I'm waiting.
eNintendo ninjas were inside the discord, watching. Now all the Yuzu devs have turned over all electronic devices, websites, logs...

senses.d: A programmer or tech worker, particularly one skilled in a particular programming language or environment; used especially in job adverts.
ex: A ninja developer can take advantage of this when building large software systems, adding a bit of C# and a dabble of Python.

senses.d: One who is considered to resemble the historical ninja in some way.
An amateur private miner in Mongolia.
Synonym of nigga, used as a friendly term of address.
ex: What's up, ninjas?
I'm thicker than a Snicker, I'm thicker than your ninja!
syn: used as a friendly term of address

senses.d: Synonym of man; used as a friendly term of address.
ex: What up, my ninja!

senses.d: Synonym of nigger.
Fast and sneaky.
ex: […]no one else would even know of such a stealthy ninja steal.

senses.d: To act or move like a ninja, particularly with regard to a combination of speed, power, and stealth.
ex: I leapt up, ninja'd over to Gav's bed and wheeched the duvet off.
In our dark house we were ninja-ing around with water guns.

senses.d: to beat someone to a post; to make the same reply just before the other party finishes typing, making their response redundant.
ex: When I hit post, I saw that Blue Emu had ninja'd me, so I just deleted my reply.

senses.d: To claim an item through abuse of game mechanics.
ex: That damn warrior ninja'd an epic-quality wand even though he can't even use it!
